name: Lorraine 'Rainy' Doucette
languages: French (Louisiana French from her grandmother, and enough Paris French to order champagne and be insulted properly)
equipment: A green satin evening gown for work, a grey tweed suit for everything else, and good shoes she cannot afford
Derringer (Remington over-and-under), 2 rounds loaded, in a garter holster or her handbag
A gold compact with a mirror she uses for watching rooms behind her

Three sets of business cards: Mrs. L. Duvall, Society Editor, Spokane Spokesman; Miss Lorraine Dupree, Northwest Casualty Mutual (claims); Mrs. Paul Haverford of Larch Hill (lent to her by a friend who is not Mrs. Haverford)
A paste diamond ring that looks real across a table and a real one, from her mother, that looks paste
A deck of cards, worn soft, and a pair of loaded dice she has never used in Port Calloway
A key to the Pelican Club's stage door
Sheet music for six songs, with the Pelican's bandleader's pencil notes
features: Knows the Block (City-Born origin: in Port Calloway she knows every back way, alley, bar and payphone and who they belong to; advantage on Streetwise checks to find a person, place or service in the city; once per foot chase she can hand the next complication to her pursuer)

The Long Con (Grifter: in downtime, a day and $20 builds a cover identity with a name, history, papers, wardrobe and one contact who will vouch for it by telephone; she can keep two covers, and has advantage on checks to keep one up)
Cheap Shot (Grifter: once per turn, an extra 2d6 damage with a finesse Melee weapon or a Sidearm when she has advantage, an ally is next to the target, or the target thinks she is harmless)
Quick Hands (Grifter, 2nd level: on each of her turns, a bonus action to Dash, Disengage or Hide, or to make one Sleight of Hand check to lift, plant or palm something)

Racket: Roper (Grifter, 3rd level: anyone she has talked to for ten minutes treats her as a friend until she gives them reason not to, and will do her a favour that costs them nothing without a check)

Back Door of Every Club (Nightclub Singer background: she can get a job singing in any club in town by tomorrow night, knows every club's back door and back room, and people tell a singer things they would never tell a cop)

personality.traits: I call everyone honey and mean it about half the time. I never sit with my back to a door or a mirror. I laugh at men's jokes before they get to the end, because I know the end. I can be anyone for an evening and I am tired, sometimes, of being myself.
personality.ideals: Everybody's running a con. The only honest thing you can do is know it, and pick your marks so they deserve it.
personality.bonds: My little brother Teddy, who is in the Navy off Korea and writes me every week on onionskin paper, and thinks I am a secretary.
personality.flaws: I cannot resist a mark with too much money and too little sense, even when I am working for someone else and it is the worst possible time. And I owe Gil Maddox four hundred dollars, which he has very kindly never mentioned.

appearance: A tall, long-necked woman of thirty-one with a cloud of dark red hair, green eyes, freckles she powders over for work, and a wide, generous mouth. On stage she is glamorous; off it she is a quick, funny, slightly tired woman in tweed who could be anyone, which is the point. Her singing voice is low and smoky; her speaking voice changes with whoever she is pretending to be.
backstory: Lorraine Doucette was born in a rooming house on Jackson Street to a Cajun mother who sang in waterfront bars and a father who left before she could remember him. She learned to sing from her mother, to read people from the bars, and to run a short con from a fourteen-year-old boy on the ferry dock who later went to prison. By twenty she was singing at the Pelican Club; by twenty-five she had been married twice, both times briefly and both times to men who deserved it, and had developed a sideline in what she calls 'social corrections': separating rich men from money they had obtained unfairly, usually from a woman. Walt Embry caught her at it in 1950, working an insurance fraud, and instead of turning her in, hired her. She still sings at the Pelican on Tuesdays and Saturdays. She knows everyone who drinks there, including Gil Maddox, who is sentimental about singers and likes her very much, and the quiet men who use the back room. She takes the Sloane job because Walt asks her and because she has always wanted to see what a district attorney looks like when he is scared.
